claim: Synthetic test cases are bootstrapped by defining dimensions across three categories (Features, Scenarios, User Personas) and generating user inputs not outputs to avoid model bias.
quote: Think about three broad categories: Features (what capabilities does your AI need to support?), Scenarios (what situations will it encounter?), and User Personas (who will be using it and how?)

claim: Synthetic data should be grounded in real system constraints (actual IDs, schedules, business rules) and you should generate inputs rather than outputs to avoid inheriting the generating model's biases.
Error analysis is the highest-ROI discovery mechanism for selecting examples, and in one case study just three issues accounted for over 60% of all problems.
quote: Error analysis - the single most valuable activity in AI development and consistently the highest-ROI activity.

claim: Structured synthetic generation starts with ~20 hand-written tuples of dimensions, then scales in two LLM steps: generate structured tuples, then convert them to natural-language queries.
quote: Start by defining dimensions: categories that describe different aspects of user queries. Each dimension captures one type of variation in user behavior.

claim: For error analysis aim to review at least 100 traces, stopping when ~20 traces yield no new failure category; review 20-50 outputs after significant changes.
quote: if ~20 traces don't turn up a new category, you can stop.

claim: The dataset grows by reviewing 100+ fresh traces each 2-4 week cycle plus 10-20 outlier traces weekly between cycles.
quote: Set a goal for reviewing at least 100+ fresh traces each review cycle. Typical review cycles range from 2-4 weeks.

claim: Sampling strategies include error-driven (prioritize negative feedback, tickets, escalations), stratified (group by user type/feature/category and sample each), and outlier (sort by metric extremes).
quote: Group traces by key dimensions (user type, feature, query category) and sample from each group.

claim: For most small to medium companies, appointing a single domain expert as a benevolent dictator to curate and label is the most effective approach.
quote: For most small to medium-sized companies, appointing a single domain expert as a 'benevolent dictator' is the most effective approach.

claim: EvalGen samples a random max of 16 responses from inputs for the human grading cycle, and developers benefit from being forced to grade a few responses before defining criteria.
quote: EvalGen takes a random sample of max 16 responses from your inputs, which limits the number of calls it needs to make per cycle.

claim: EvalGen asks humans to grade a subset of LLM outputs and uses that feedback to select assertion implementations (code or LLM-grader prompts) that better align with user grades.
quote: EvalGen asks humans to grade a subset of LLM outputs; this feedback is used to select implementations that better align with user grades.

claim: Synthetic eval test cases proved as effective as hand-crafted data for refining criteria and aligning with human preferences, with 83% of N=24 participants preferring synthetic generation over manual creation.
quote: generated synthetic data proved as effective as hand-crafted data for both refining evaluation criteria and aligning with user expectations.

claim: Effective synthetic generation is configurable by domain, persona, and length, and deliberately includes ambiguous, partially-matching, and out-of-domain borderline cases to expose blind spots.
quote: generating ambiguous, partially matching, and out-of-domain examples is important to identify blind spots.

claim: Vendor guidance treats golden datasets as living artifacts: start with a focused representative set covering core use cases and edge cases, then continuously pull validated production traces back in.
quote: Start with a focused set of representative inputs and carefully validated expected outputs, covering your core use cases and known edge cases.

claim: Quality beats quantity for golden datasets, and stale examples give false confidence so production data must be integrated continuously.
quote: Building one well matters more than building one with a large amount of data.

claim: Braintrust converts production traces and reported failures into eval datasets and regression tests in one click, while LangSmith requires manual curation between tracing and evaluation.
quote: Braintrust can turn production traces into eval datasets with one click, building regression tests from real failures and edge cases, not synthetic examples.
